prompt: Match each anomaly to what goes wrong.

pairs.right: A rename that stops halfway leaves two names
A department cannot exist until it has a book
Deleting the last book erases the department

right_distractors: A query reads more columns than it needs

prompt: Why are the anomalies normalisation prevents mostly absent from Ana's warehouse?

choices.text: One load writes it, in batches, in a transaction
choices.why: Right. Many writers at random moments is what makes anomalies; the warehouse has one.

choices.text: DuckDB has no UPDATE statement
choices.why: It has one; section 04 used it.

choices.text: The warehouse has no repeated values at all
choices.why: It repeats on purpose: the department on every book row.

choices.text: Warehouses never store text that people might want to rename later
choices.why: Departments get renamed; the load carries the new name.

prompt: Of the three costs a join puts on a reader, which one does a columnar engine make small?
hint: Two of them are about people.

choices.text: Knowing which tables to join
choices.why: That is knowledge in somebody's head; no engine removes it.

choices.text: Getting the join condition right
choices.why: A wrong condition runs fast and returns the wrong total.

choices.text: Time
choices.why: Right. Small dimensions are cheap to join; the other two costs remain.

choices.text: None of them; joins are always expensive
choices.why: Section 06 measured them as nearly free here.

prompt: "Denormalising moves the cost from every query to the load." What exactly does the load do once that each query would otherwise do?
hint: Think of the department of a book.

choices.text: It caches the results of every report
choices.why: That is an aggregate, and only for the reports someone built it for.

choices.text: It works out each book's department, correctly, and writes it on the row
choices.why: Right. Every query after that reads a column instead of walking the tree.

choices.text: It removes the category table
choices.why: Staging still holds it; the star just does not make readers use it.

choices.text: It indexes every column
choices.why: Indexes are not what this lesson is about.

prompt: How many rows of the wide table does renaming *Non-fiction* write?
The rename of the wide table was interrupted after 2025. What would every report grouped by department have shown?
hint: Look at the two rows of the result.

choices.text: An error, because the table was locked
choices.why: Nothing locks it once the statement stops.

choices.text: The old name only, until the update finished
choices.why: 2025 already said `Nonfiction`.

choices.text: The right totals, because the sum is the same
choices.why: The grand total is the same; the department's row is split in two.

choices.text: Two rows for one department, split by year
choices.why: Right. The update anomaly, inside a warehouse.

prompt: What is the safe way to change a name in the wide table?

choices.text: Update it in place, one year at a time, during the night when nobody is reading
choices.why: That is the interrupted update, slowed down.

choices.text: Add a second column with the new name and leave the old one
choices.why: Two columns for one fact is the anomaly by design.

choices.text: Rebuild it from the star
choices.why: Right. A derived copy is rebuilt, never edited.

choices.text: Ask the report tool to rename it on display
choices.why: Then every tool has to know, and the data still says the old name.

prompt: In PostgreSQL the star took 85 MB and the wide table 242 MB. How many times larger is the wide table? Give one decimal.
Why does the wide table cost 2.8 times the star by row and only 1.3 times in Parquet?
hint: What does a column of department names look like?

choices.text: A column of repeated values compresses to almost nothing
choices.why: Right. Lesson 8 shows the encodings; the repetition that triples a row store barely moves a column store.

choices.text: Parquet drops duplicate rows
choices.why: No row is dropped; the 887,477 are all there.

choices.text: PostgreSQL stores text twice
choices.why: It stores it once per row, in full.

choices.text: The wide table has fewer columns in Parquet
choices.why: Same 31 columns.

prompt: The star answered in 0.021 s and the wide table in 0.017 s. What is the fair reading?
hint: One run each, on a shared machine.

choices.text: The wide table is about 20% faster and should replace the star
choices.why: One run each cannot show a 20% difference, and speed is not the only cost.

choices.text: The star is slower because it has more rows
choices.why: It has the same 887,477 fact rows and small dimensions.

choices.text: DuckDB cached the second query
choices.why: They were different queries in different runs.

choices.text: About the same: joins to small dimensions are cheap here
choices.why: Right. The difference is the size of the noise.

prompt: Which of these are real costs of a one big table? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It must be rebuilt rather than edited
choices.why: Yes. Section 04 showed what editing it does.

choices.text: It holds one grain only
choices.why: Yes. Stock and payments are not in a table of sale lines.

choices.text: A new attribute means a new column on the biggest table
choices.why: Yes, rebuilt from scratch.

choices.text: Tools that read one table at a time cannot use it
choices.why: Those are exactly the tools it suits.

prompt: In Inmon's design, what do people query?

choices.text: The normalised warehouse directly
choices.why: Inmon puts marts in front of it.

choices.text: Dimensional data marts built from the normalised warehouse
choices.why: Right. The core is the source of truth; marts are for reading.

choices.text: The hubs and satellites
choices.why: Those are Data Vault.

choices.text: The operational database
choices.why: Lesson 1 argued against that.

prompt: Match each school to its integrated core.
A bank has forty source systems, changes them every quarter, and its auditors ask which load wrote each number. Which design does the lesson suggest fits it best underneath its marts?
hint: Inserts only, and every row stamped.

choices.text: A Data Vault
choices.why: Right. New sources are new satellites, and every row says which load brought it.

choices.text: One big table
choices.why: It records nothing about loads and is rebuilt wholesale.

choices.text: Kimball stars alone
choices.why: Workable, but conforming forty changing sources and auditing loads is where a vault helps.

choices.text: The operational databases themselves
choices.why: Forty of them, in forty shapes, with no history.

prompt: What does a hub hold?

choices.text: Descriptive attributes with their history
choices.why: Those are satellites.

choices.text: Relationships between keys
choices.why: Those are links.

choices.text: Business keys, with when and where they were first loaded
choices.why: Right. One row per customer number, per ISBN.

choices.text: Pre-summed totals
choices.why: Those are aggregates, outside the vault.

prompt: Why does nobody report from a Data Vault directly?
hint: Look at the query for the current tier.

choices.text: Vaults are too small to report from
choices.why: They are larger than stars, not smaller.

choices.text: Every question needs joins and a window to find each latest row
choices.why: Right. That is why marts are built on top of it.

choices.text: Its data is encrypted with md5
choices.why: md5 makes a key, not a secret.

choices.text: It holds no history
choices.why: It holds all of it.

prompt: In a Data Vault, descriptive attributes and their changes live in tables called ___.
How many rows does `agg_sales_month` hold?
Which rule keeps an aggregate from disagreeing with the source about the data?

choices.text: It is loaded straight from the operational database
choices.why: Then it could disagree with the fact table.

choices.text: It is stored in a separate database
choices.why: Where it is stored changes nothing.

choices.text: It has no dimension keys
choices.why: It keeps the conformed ones, rolled up.

choices.text: It is built from the atomic fact table
choices.why: Right. Derived, never loaded from the source.

prompt: After the correction, the fact table and the aggregate differ by 1,000 centavos. What is wrong with the aggregate?

choices.text: It rounds every month to the nearest ten reais
choices.why: It summed exact centavos; it matched to the centavo before.

choices.text: It counts cancelled orders
choices.why: It was built from the same fact table.

choices.text: It is as old as its last rebuild
choices.why: Right. A copy is only as fresh as the moment it was made.

choices.text: DuckDB corrupted it
choices.why: Nothing is corrupt; it is stale.

prompt: Put the steps of a load that keeps an aggregate true in order.
hint: Detail first, summary second, check last.
items: Load the corrected rows into the fact table
Rebuild the aggregate from the fact table
Compare the two totals, and fail the load if they differ
trap: Checking before rebuilding would fail every load that changed anything.

prompt: A team keeps a table of product prices that several applications update a row at a time all day. Should it be denormalised into the products' rows?

choices.text: No: many writers, row at a time
choices.why: Right. Normalise what many write; the anomalies are real there.

choices.text: Yes, repetition is cheap in a column store
choices.why: Storage is not the issue when many writers can leave it half updated.

choices.text: Yes, and add an aggregate as well
choices.why: That adds a second copy to keep in step.

choices.text: Only if it is in Parquet
choices.why: The format does not change who writes it.

prompt: Normalise what is written by many, denormalise what is read by many, and never edit a ___.
hint: A wide table or an aggregate is one.

prompt: A dashboard tool can only read one table. What should Ana give it?

choices.text: Replace the star with a wide table
choices.why: Then every other process and grain loses its model.

choices.text: The staging tables
choices.why: Nothing outside the load reads staging.

choices.text: A wide table that analysts correct by hand when they spot errors
choices.why: Editing a copy is how the anomaly comes back.

choices.text: A wide table rebuilt from the star after every load
choices.why: Right. An output of the warehouse, not its foundation.

prompt: Which statement about storage and normalisation is supported by this lesson's measurements?

choices.text: Repetition costs the same everywhere
choices.why: It cost 2.8 times in one and 1.3 in the other.

choices.text: The space argument for normalising is strong by row and weak by column
choices.why: Right. 2.8 times against 1.3 times.

choices.text: Parquet makes the wide table smaller than the star
choices.why: Smaller than by row, still larger than the star.

choices.text: PostgreSQL compresses repetition better
choices.why: It was the one where the wide table tripled.
